Maladaptive Strategies.value: try hard not think about the trauma
Going out at night or being outside after dark
Any form of physical contact with others

Memory.value: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

vignette: Kofi had always been drawn to the detective work for its sense of control and order. But that was before he was taken captive by a group of armed men while on an undercover operation in a rough neighborhood. For three days, he was held in a cramped, dimly lit room with no windows, forced to listen to the sound of his own heartbeat and the muffled voices of his captors. The experience left Kofi with memories that he couldn't shake. Sometimes, when he least expected it, he would hear the sound of footsteps echoing down a hallway or the rustle of fabric that sounded eerily like the ropes that bound him. These auditory recall episodes were always fleeting, but they left him breathless and disoriented. He knew exactly what had happened to him, but when he tried to describe it to his girlfriend, Nia, or even just to himself, he found that words failed him. The memories felt stuck in his throat, refusing to be articulated. As a result of these unsettling recollections, Kofi started to develop maladaptive strategies to cope with the emotional intensity they brought up. He tried hard not to think about the trauma, pushing the thoughts away whenever they arose. At night, he would find excuses to stay indoors, avoiding the darkness that seemed to amplify his anxiety. Physical contact with others also became increasingly uncomfortable for him; even Nia's gentle touch made him flinch. Kofi knew these strategies were probably not healthy in the long run, but they provided a temporary reprieve from the emotional turmoil that threatened to overwhelm him. He felt like he was walking on eggshells, never knowing when the next auditory recall episode would strike or what memories would come flooding back. His work as a detective suffered as well; he found himself avoiding cases that involved nighttime stakeouts or confrontations with potentially violent suspects. Despite his best efforts, Kofi couldn't shake the feeling of being trapped, even in his own home. He would sometimes wake up in the middle of the night, drenched in sweat, with the sound of his captors' voices still echoing in his ears. It was as if he had never truly escaped that cramped room. Nia noticed the change in Kofi and encouraged him to seek help. At first, he resisted, thinking that he just needed time to "get over it." But the memories persisted, and so did the maladaptive strategies. Eventually, he realized that he couldn't keep living like this, constantly looking over his shoulder, waiting for the other shoe to drop. That's when Kofi decided to seek professional help, hoping to break free from the grip of his traumatic past and reclaim control over his life. He was afraid of what the therapy might uncover, but more than that, he was tired of being held captive by his memories.
